description: From the United States to India, via Europe, populist leaders are shaking up traditional parties. Why is this wave affecting **almost all democracies** at the same time?

hero.hook: The people against the elites: a discourse more than a century old, but which has never been so convincing.

blocks.text: Since the 2010s, **populism** is no longer a marginal phenomenon. From the United States to India, via Europe and Latin America, leaders are shaking up the traditional parties that have been in power for decades.
This movement does not come out of nowhere. It is rooted in very real economic, cultural and technological divides. This course explores the logic of this discourse and the reasons for its rise.

Populism is not defined by a precise economic program, but by a very particular political logic. According to political scientist Jan-Werner Müller, its central idea is the : there would be only one “real people”, and the populist leader would be its sole spokesperson. [[monism]]

blocks.caption: The populist discourse divides society into two opposing camps.

blocks.text: This vision divides society into two camps: on one side, a “pure people”, bearers of authentic values, on the other, a “corrupt elite”, accused of betraying the general interest. This framework is very flexible: on the right, the people are often defined by the nation, opposed to an elite considered too globalist. On the left, it is defined by social class, facing a financial elite.

The very first major modern populist party, the American People's Party in 1892, already called for nationalizing the railroads, because farmers believed that rates were set by an invisible financial elite.

sections.title: The pure people against the corrupt elite

blocks.text: Several crises come together to explain this rise. On the economic front, researcher Branko Milanović showed that between 1988 and 2008, the Asian middle classes and the richest in the world saw their incomes increase, while the Western middle classes stagnated. This feeling of being downgraded fueled lasting anger.

blocks.caption: The 2015 migration crisis has fueled a feeling of identity insecurity in Europe.

blocks.text: Added to this economic divide is a cultural divide: the acceleration of societal changes and the migratory crisis of 2015 have created identity insecurity among many voters, who feel more distant from the decisions made by urban elites.

Finally, social networks have transformed political communication. They reinforce polarization and allow leaders to speak directly to their audiences, with simple and emotional language, without going through traditional media.

The global political landscape offers a great diversity of populist figures. Donald Trump transformed the American Republican Party around protectionism and nationalism. In Hungary, Viktor Orbán has built a , where the election results justify an increasing concentration of power. [[Illiberal democracies (Orbán)]]

blocks.caption: Very different figures share the same rhetoric of breaking with the elites.

blocks.text: In France, Marine Le Pen pursued a  strategy to expand her electorate, while maintaining a discourse centered on national preference. Left-wing populism, embodied by Jean-Luc Mélenchon in France or Bernie Sanders in the United States, rather favors the redistribution of wealth, but shares the same rhetoric of breaking with the “system”. [[demonization]]

sections.title: Very different faces, the same method

blocks.text: The great paradox of populism appears once it comes to power. The leader can no longer be content with being the opponent of the system: he becomes the system. To maintain his image as a rebel, he often appoints new enemies, such as judges or civil servants, accused of blocking his will.

This is where the risk for institutions becomes concrete. In Hungary and Poland, reforms aimed to reduce the independence of the judiciary. In the event of electoral defeat, some leaders even challenge the legitimacy of the vote, as during the attack on the Capitol in 2021.

One of the most popular presidents of the United States, Andrew Jackson, was nicknamed "King Mob" by his detractors because he opened the White House to the people for a party that ended in a near-riot.
But this rise also acts as a useful alarm signal: it forces traditional parties to take up neglected issues, such as industrial sovereignty or public services in rural areas.

Populism divides the world into “pure people” versus “corrupt elite”. It has been rising everywhere since 2010, driven by inequalities linked to globalization and cultural insecurity amplified by social networks.

sections.title: The real test: the exercise of power
